newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM Gujral reaches out to his public.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM Gujral reaches out to his public.

text.p: Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral took up a time-honoured tradition among India's rulers on Friday by inviting members of the public into his home to listen to their grievances.

Gujral, 77, who took over as India's 12th premier last month, listened patiently for over two hours to the woes of more than 500 people who crowded into the compound of his heavily guarded home in an elite New Delhi neighbourhood.
A young couple who visited Gujral said they had come only to be photographed with him. Namrita, an 11-year-old girl, said she wanted his autograph on a picture she had drawn.
"I felt thrilled," said Vijay Kumar, after asking Gujral to help him find a government job.
Arvind Razdan, a 24-year-old, burst into tears as he held out his petition for admission in a government-run training centre.

Modern-day Indian politicians are simply following the press-the-flesh populism set down by generations of kings. The Mughals built special halls in their palaces called "Diwan-e-Aam" (hall of the people) where they held public audiences and dispensed justice and favours.

Gujral has decreed that any commoner can get past his bodyguards on Friday mornings. Hordes of pedestrians ran pell-mell through peak-hour traffic near the prime minister's official residence as word spread of the newest durbar (audience) in town.
Flanked by officials, Gujral passed instant orders on several petitions, but politely turned down pleas for job transfers from some of India's legions of government employees.

Later he told reporters: "I want to give the message that this government at least listens to the grievances and problems of the people. It may not be immediately possible to resolve their problems but they should at least be heard."
